body.text: Section 194 of Canada's Income Tax Act, in Part VIII, imposes a refundable 50% tax on a corporation that designates an amount under subsection 194(4) for shares, debt obligations or rights it issued under the 1983 Scientific Research Tax Credit (SRTC). The investor claims the matching credit under section 127.3, and the corporation recovers the tax as Part VIII refunds as it spends on SR&ED. No new designations have been possible since the mid-1980s.
Executive Overview of Part VIII and the Scientific Research Tax

Part VIII of the federal Income Tax Act (ITA), R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.), is titled "Refundable Tax on Corporations in Respect of Scientific Research and Experimental Development Tax Credit". It consists of two sections. Section 194 imposes the tax, defines the Part VIII refund and the refundable Part VIII tax on hand, and sets the rules for designating amounts. Section 195 governs returns, payment, interest and a set of anti-avoidance rules.

Part VIII is the issuer-side half of the Scientific Research Tax Credit (SRTC), a financing mechanism introduced in the 1983 federal budget. Under the SRTC, a corporation carrying on research could raise money by issuing shares, debt obligations or rights to outside investors and designating an amount in respect of each instrument. The investor then claimed a credit under section 127.3, and the issuing corporation paid a tax under Part VIII equal to 50% of the designated amount. That tax was refundable: the corporation recovered it as it incurred qualifying scientific research and experimental development (SR&ED) expenditures.

The SRTC was abolished in 1985 after it gave outside investors about $1.6 billion in tax relief between 1983 and 1985 without evidence that the money was reinvested in research. Subsection 194(4.2) now bars designations for instruments issued after the statutory cutoffs, subject to transitional relief that ended by 1986. Sections 194 and 195 nevertheless remain in the consolidated Act, so practitioners still meet them when reviewing legacy corporate histories, reading cross-references in section 127.3, or distinguishing the old "SR&ED tax credit" from the modern investment tax credit (ITC) under section 127.

The practical conclusion for current claimants is that Part VIII imposes no filing or payment obligation unless a corporation made a designation under subsection 194(4). A business claiming SR&ED today does so through the subsection 37(1) expenditure pool and the ITC under subsection 127(5) and section 127.1, not through Part VIII.

body.text: Historical Context: The 1983 Scientific Research Tax Credit
Policy Design and the Flow-Through Mechanism

By the early 1980s, Canada had offered tax incentives for research for many years. A scientific research tax credit of 5% to 10% of current and capital expenditures, varying with the type of company and the region where the work was done, was introduced in 1977. These credits had limited value to start-up and loss-making research corporations, which had little or no tax payable to absorb them.

The 1983 budget responded with the SRTC. A company could enter into research contracts on behalf of an outside investor who had acquired its shares or debt securities for SR&ED purposes. The issuing company designated an amount in respect of each instrument, the investor received a credit of 50% of the investment, and the company gave up its own tax incentives on the related spending. In effect, the SRTC let a research corporation without taxable income sell its tax incentive to investors who could use it. The Department of Finance's 1983 technical notes describe the financing mechanism under new section 127.3 and the special refundable tax the issuing corporation paid under Part VIII.
The "Quick Flip" and the Cost to Federal Revenue

The mechanism was open to abuse. In the "quick flip" transaction, an issuer that had designated an amount for a debenture or other instrument would redeem it almost at once, leaving the investor with the credit and returning most of the cash. Revenue Canada treated these arrangements as a serious concern, and they produced litigation that ran well into the late 1980s. The Library of Parliament reports that the SRTC let outside investors turn a quick profit, that the tax savings were not shown to have been reinvested in SR&ED, and that outside investors received about $1.6 billion in tax relief between 1983 and 1985. Later policy studies identify the SRTC experience as one of the reasons Canada's current SR&ED program was built the way it was.
Termination and Transitional Cutoffs
The SRTC was eliminated in 1985. The statutory cutoffs are set out in subsection 194(4.2), which lists the instruments for which no amount may be designated:

items: shares issued after October 10, 1984, and shares, debt obligations or rights issued or granted after that date, subject to exceptions for written agreements entered into before October 11, 1984 and for arrangements that were substantially advanced by October 10, 1984;

certain qualifying shares, where transitional rules preserved designations for shares issued before May 23, 1985, or issued after May 22, 1985 and before 1986 under an agreement made before May 23, 1985, and for issues under a prospectus or registration statement filed before May 24, 1985;
shares, debt obligations or rights issued or granted by an excluded corporation (as defined in subsection 127.1(2)) after June 15, 1984.

body.text: Subsection 194(4) separately excludes shares or rights issued before October 1983 and shares already designated under subsection 192(4), the Part VII share-purchase tax credit. Read together, these rules mean no designation can be made today, and Part VIII applies only to amounts already designated within the transitional windows.
From the SRTC to the Modern SR&ED Program

In 1985, the federal government replaced the SRTC with incentives paid directly to the performer. The small-business credit became fully refundable on current expenditures for the first $2 million of R&D performed by an associated group, Revenue Canada was required to validate claims at assessment, and a specialized assessing and audit group and a standard prescribed claim form were created. In 1986, the term "scientific research and experimental development" was added to section 2900 of the Income Tax Regulations, buildings were excluded from eligible expenditures, and the refundable credit for small CCPCs was kept at 35%. These reforms are the origin of today's program, which is administered by the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) and delivers credits only to the taxpayer that carries on or pays for the SR&ED.

body.text: Subsection 194(1): The 50% Charging Provision

Every corporation must pay a tax under Part VIII for a taxation year equal to 50% of the total of all amounts it designated under subsection 194(4) in respect of shares or debt obligations issued, or rights granted, by it in the year. The rate mirrors the 50% credit available to a corporate investor under section 127.3, so the tax paid by the issuer matches the credit received by the investor. Because the tax is refundable, it worked as a deposit held by the Crown until the issuer showed that the funds raised had been spent on research.
Subsections 194(2) and 194(3): The Part VIII Refund and Refundable Part VIII Tax on Hand
A corporation's Part VIII refund for a taxation year is the lesser of two amounts:

items: the total of (i) the amount by which the corporation's own SR&ED tax credit for the year exceeds the amount it deducted under subsection 127.3(1) from its Part I tax, and (ii) an amount the corporation claims, not exceeding 50% of the amount by which its qualifying expenditures exceed the amounts already used; and
the corporation's refundable Part VIII tax on hand at the end of the year.

body.text: The qualifying expenditures in clause 194(2)(a)(ii)(A) are expenditures made after April 19, 1983, in the year or the preceding year, of a kind described in paragraph 37(1)(a) or 37(1)(b), other than prescribed expenditures excluded from "qualified expenditure" in subsection 127(9). Clause (B) removes prior-year expenditures that already supported a Part VIII refund, a subsection 37(1) deduction or a subsection 127(5) deduction, and clause (C) removes twice the portion of any section 37.1 deduction relating to those expenditures. The result is that each dollar of SR&ED spending can unlock 50 cents of refund once, and cannot also be deducted from income or used for an ITC.

Refundable Part VIII tax on hand, defined in subsection 194(3), is the total of Part VIII taxes payable for the year and all preceding years, less Part VIII refunds for preceding years. It works as a running balance: designations add to it, refunds reduce it, and the refund for a year can never exceed it.
Subsections 194(4) to 194(4.2): Designation Rules

Any taxable Canadian corporation may designate an amount in respect of a share or debt obligation it issued, or a right it granted, by filing the prescribed form with the Minister on or before the last day of the month following the month of issuance or grant. The designated amount may not exceed the consideration received for the instrument. For shares, the consideration is reduced by any assistance from a government, municipality or other public authority, other than amounts included in computing the SR&ED tax credit for that share. Subsection 194(4.1) then adjusts the paid-up capital of designated shares, and subsection 194(4.2) sets the cutoffs discussed above.
Subsections 194(5) to 194(9): Timing, Financing Contracts and Late Designations

Subsection 194(5) deems a Part VIII refund to be a payment on account of Part VIII tax made on the last day of the second month after the end of the year. This matters for interest, because it fixes when the refund offsets an outstanding liability. Subsection 194(6) defines a "financing contract" as a written contract under which a person pays a corporation for a right to receive income other than interest or dividends, which brought royalty-style research financings within the regime.

Subsection 194(7) allows a late designation to be treated as made on time if the prescribed form is filed and the related tax is paid within three years, and the Minister may require these steps by notice within 90 days. Subsection 194(8) imposes a penalty for late designation of 1% of the designated amount for each month, capped at $500 per month, and subsection 194(9) prevents a second designation for an instrument once an amount has been designated.
The Investor Side: Section 127.3 SR&ED Tax Credit
Computation of the Credit

Section 127.3 is the counterpart to Part VIII. Subsection 127.3(1) allows a taxpayer to deduct from tax otherwise payable an amount up to its SR&ED tax credit for the year plus its unused SR&ED tax credit for the following year. Under subsection 127.3(2), the SR&ED tax credit is computed as A minus B, where A is the total of amounts designated under subsection 194(4) for shares, debt obligations or rights the taxpayer first acquired (other than as a broker or dealer), multiplied by 50% for a corporation or 34% for an individual other than a trust. Element B covers amounts that subsection 127.3(5) requires a cooperative corporation to deduct.

The unused SR&ED tax credit is the credit for the year less the taxpayer's Part I tax otherwise payable (or, where the minimum tax in Division E.1 applies, the excess of that tax over the minimum amount under section 127.51) and less its refundable Part VIII tax on hand. A corporation that both issued and acquired designated instruments therefore had to coordinate its section 127.3 credit with its Part VIII balance.
Cost Base Reduction, Trusts and Partnerships

Subsection 127.3(6) reduces the investor's cost of the share, debt obligation or right by 50% of the designated amount. Where the reduction exceeds the cost, the excess is a capital gain for capital property or income otherwise, and the cost is deemed to be nil. Subsections 127.3(3) and (4) attribute designated amounts to trust beneficiaries and partnership members, and subsection 127.3(3.1) excludes employee benefit plan trusts, revoked deferred profit sharing plans and trusts exempt under section 149. The remaining subsections of section 127.3 also include the consideration for a designation in the investor's acquisition cost without including it in the issuer's income.

body.text: Where the issuer never spent the funds on research, the Part VIII tax stayed with the Crown while the investor kept its credit. That outcome put the economic cost on the issuer, which is why the "quick flip" and related arrangements depended on the issuer having nothing to lose, and why section 195 added specific anti-avoidance rules.
Section 195: Returns, Payment, Interest and Anti-Avoidance
Filing, Payment and Interest

A corporation liable to Part VIII tax must file a return for the year in prescribed form by the date its Part I return is due, under subsection 195(1). Subsection 195(2) requires it to pay, on account of the tax, 50% of the amounts designated by the last day of the month following the month in which the instrument was issued or the right granted, so payment falls due at the same time as the designation form. Subsections 195(3) and (4) charge interest at the prescribed rate on unpaid amounts and set the deemed instalment rules used to compute it.

body.text: These rules were drafted in response to the abuses described above. Subsection 195(5) protects the Crown by moving the loss to an investor who knew, or ought to have known, that the issuer was evading the tax. Subsection 195(7.1) catches over-reporting of designated amounts in the information returns that supported investors' claims.
Subsection 195(8): Part I Provisions Applied to Part VIII

Subsection 195(8) applies sections 151, 152, 158 and 159, subsection 161(11), sections 162 to 167 (other than subsections 164(1.1) to (1.3)) and Division J of Part I to Part VIII, with any modifications the circumstances require. As a result, the ordinary rules for assessment, reassessment, collection, penalties, refunds and objections and appeals govern Part VIII tax, and the Minister may assess an amount payable under Part VIII before the end of the year.
Relationship to the Modern SR&ED Provisions
Distinguishing the SRTC from the Investment Tax Credit

The Act still uses the term "scientific research and experimental development tax credit" in section 127.3 and Part VIII, which can be confused with the modern SR&ED ITC. The two are separate. The section 127.3 credit is earned by an investor that bought a designated instrument, while the ITC under subsection 127(9) is earned by the taxpayer that incurs qualified SR&ED expenditures. Likewise, a Part VIII refund returns a tax the issuer itself paid, while a refundable investment tax credit under section 127.1 pays out a credit earned on the claimant's own spending.

body.text: Shared Definitions and Cross-References

Part VIII relies on the same expenditure categories as the modern program. The refund formula in subsection 194(2) draws on paragraphs 37(1)(a) and (b) and on the "qualified expenditure" definition in subsection 127(9), and it excludes expenditures already deducted under subsection 37(1) or claimed under subsection 127(5). The meaning of SR&ED itself comes from the definition in subsection 248(1). When reading an old Part VIII file, it helps to remember that these provisions have been amended many times since 1985, so the version in force for the relevant year must be used rather than the current text.
Practical Implications for Taxpayers and Advisers
Current SR&ED Claimants

A corporation claiming SR&ED today has no Part VIII return to file and no Part VIII tax to pay unless it made a designation under subsection 194(4), which is no longer possible for new instruments. The relevant rules for a current claim are the SR&ED expenditure pool under section 37, the ITC under section 127, refundability under section 127.1 and the reporting deadline in subsection 37(11). A Canadian-controlled private corporation (CCPC) looking for cash from its research should look to the refundable ITC under section 127.1, which serves the purpose the SRTC was meant to serve, a cash return for research corporations without tax payable.
Legacy Files and Corporate History

Part VIII still matters in a few situations. Corporations that issued designated instruments in 1983 to 1986 may carry adjusted paid-up capital under subsection 194(4.1), and investors' cost bases in those instruments were reduced under subsection 127.3(6), which affects gains on any later disposition. Due diligence on long-established research corporations, amalgamated entities or old holding structures can turn up these adjustments. The Department of Finance's 1983 notes also show consequential amendments to the capital cost base, amalgamation and winding-up rules made when the SRTC was introduced.
Reading the Statute Correctly

Readers sometimes treat Part VIII as a live tax on current SR&ED claimants or confuse the section 127.3 credit with the 35% enhanced ITC. Neither is correct. When a question refers to "Part VIII tax" or "section 194", the first step is to confirm whether any designation was ever made, and the second is to identify the version of the Act in force for the year concerned. Questions about current credits belong under sections 37, 127 and 127.1.
Conclusions

Section 194 and Part VIII are a closed chapter in Canada's R&D tax history, but not an empty one. They set out a complete regime: a 50% refundable tax on designating corporations, a spending-based refund, strict designation timelines and penalties, and anti-avoidance rules in section 195 aimed at the abuses that ended the SRTC. With no new designations possible, their practical role is limited to legacy capital and cost base adjustments and to understanding why the modern SR&ED program delivers its incentives directly to the performer.

For any current claim, the advice is to apply the section 37 pool, the section 127 ITC and section 127.1 refundability, and to treat Part VIII as background. For legacy files, the advice is to confirm whether a subsection 194(4) designation was made, apply the version of sections 127.3, 194 and 195 in force for the relevant year, and trace any paid-up capital and cost base adjustments through to the present.
